# SIMS and HR-XPS characterization of lithiated graphite from the

# magnetic fusion device RFX-mod

B. Rais1, E. T. Ostrowski2, A. Canton3, C.H. Skinner1, S. Barison4, S. Fiameni4, B. E. Koel2

1 Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, Princeton, NJ, 08543, USA

2Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, NJ, 08540, USA

3Consorzio RFX, C.so Stati Uniti 4, 35127, Padova, Italy

4CNR ICMATE, C.so Stati Uniti 4, 35127, Padova, Italy

## Abstract

Lithium wall conditioning has improved the performance of many magnetic fusion devices. Li

conditioning in the RFX-mod device was performed by: (1) a single Li pellet injector and (2)

a multi-Li pellet injector during He plasma discharges; (3) a Li evaporator after He glow

discharge cleaning and He plasma discharge exposure. This report compares the spatial and

depth distributions of Li deposited on polycrystalline graphite witness samples at different

locations in RFX-mod and the elemental and chemical compositions of the resulting surfaces.

The sample surfaces were analyzed ex situ using secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) and

high-resolution X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (HR-XPS). The results showed that Li pellet

injection provided a relatively uniform toroidal coverage while Li evaporation produced highly

localized Li deposition. A Li 1s HR-XPS peak at 56.5 eV binding energy (BE) characteristic

of lithium-intercalated graphite was only observed with the sample exposed to Li evaporation.

All of the samples exhibited a HR-XPS C 1s peak at 285.1-285.2 eV BE that is largely

attributed to hydrogenated graphite. This finding suggests that hydrogenation of fresh graphite

occurs during He plasma discharge exposures. Our results have implications for density control

and the selection of Li conditioning techniques in magnetic fusion devices.

## 1. Introduction

Wall materials inside a magnetic fusion device interact with the plasma and strongly influence

plasma performance. Coating the plasma facing components (PFCs) with Li in a process

referred to as Li conditioning, or lithiumization, has improved plasma performance in devices

such as TFTR [1], T-11M [2], FTU [3], CDX-U [4], NSTX [5], LTX [6], EAST [7], and DIII-

D [8]. Benefits observed after lithiumization include increased confinement time, reduced H

isotope recycling, reduced impurity emissions, and suppressed edge-localized modes (ELMs).

The reduction in H isotope recycling is attributed in part to the high chemical reactivity of Li,

which results in incident H binding to Li, or Li-bound O, rather than recycling back into the

plasma [9–11].

Li conditioning has been performed by a variety of methods across magnetic fusion devices,

with each technique providing varying spatial uniformity and Li injection rates. Methods of

lithiumization include pellet injection [1], powder injection [7,8,12], evaporation [4,6,7,13,14],

liquid lithium limiter (LLL) comprised of a capillary porous system (CPS) [2–4], and flowing

liquid lithium systems [15]. The RFX-mod device has experimented with several Li

conditioning techniques, including a single Li pellet injector (LPI) [16], Li evaporation via a

capillary porous system [17], and a multi-pellet Li injector (MPI) [18].

RFX-mod is a reversed field pinch (RFP) magnetic fusion device of circular cross section and

major/minor radius of 2/0.46 m that operates at high plasma currents up to 2 MA [19]. RFX-

mod does not have a limiter or divertor, resulting in plasmas that interact with the entirety of

the vessel walls. Tiles made of polycrystalline graphite (manufactured by Carbone Lorraine,

type 5890PT) completely cover the first wall of RFX-mod in order to withstand heat loads that

can locally reach tens of MW/m2 [20].

Graphite PFCs are known to retain large quantities of hydrogen [21,22]. Incident H ions and

atoms that are not reflected face a complex transport and chemical environment within the

graphite tiles. Upon implantation, H atoms diffuse along graphitic planes, grain boundaries,

and porous channels and eventually recombine into H2 molecules in the bulk or at the surface

or chemisorb (form chemical bonds) to C atoms in graphitic planes or at defects [21,23–25]. H

chemisorption to graphitic C atoms results in the rehybridization of the sp2-hybridized C-C

bonds to sp3-hybridized C-H bonds [26–31]. The C-H bonds in graphite are stable at room

temperature but can be broken by elevated temperatures (T > 400 K) or by ion bombardment

to yield the desorption of H2 molecules [21,24,25,29,30,32,33].

As graphite PFCs in fusion devices continually accumulate hydrogen and eventually saturate

during plasma discharges, the recycling of H back into the plasma poses problems for density

control. Many fusion devices with graphite PFCs, including RFX-mod, addressed density

control problems by implementing He glow discharge cleaning (GDC) to reduce the H

inventory in the graphite [34–38]. The Li conditioning techniques previously described also

help control plasma density and supplement He GDC. Injected Li is well-known to intercalate

into graphite and is ionized in the process by donating an electron to the delocalized network

of  bonds in graphite [39–42].

Ex situ surface analysis studies used secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) and X-ray

photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to characterize the spatial and depth distribution and

chemical composition of films produced by lithiumization in RFX-mod [18,43]. Similar

investigations of boronization in RFX-mod utilized SIMS, XPS, and Fourier Transform

infrared attenuated total reflection (FTIR-ATR) spectroscopy to demonstrate toroidal

variations in boron film thickness and film stoichiometry related to sample distance from the

boronization glow discharge electrodes [44]. Such RFX-mod sample exposure experiments can

be compared to ex situ surface analysis studies performed utilizing DIII-D’s Divertor Material

Analysis System (DiMES) [45] or the in-vacuo surface analysis studies performed with the

Materials Analysis and Particle Probe (MAPP) on LTX [46] and NSTX [47] or with the Sample

Exposure Probe (SEP) on LTX- [48]. Other studies have used ex situ surface analysis to

investigate the composition or erosion of samples taken directly from multiple PFC tiles after

surface conditioning and plasma exposure in NSTX [49,50] and DIII-D [51].

Our studies presented herein compare the spatial and depth distribution and the final chemical

state of Li films deposited by the LPI, CPS, and MPI lithiumization methods in RFX-mod by

using SIMS and high-resolution XPS (HR-XPS). We describe first an examination of the

spatial and depth distribution of lithium deposition around the RFX-mod torus obtained by

different Li injection techniques. Second, we report on the lithium abundance and elemental

composition of the first wall surfaces. Lastly, chemical interactions of lithium with RFX-mod

graphite and in-vessel and atmospheric impurities were investigated. These results are relevant

to discussions of Li conditioning, density control, and H recycling in magnetic fusion devices

with graphite PFCs, including the newly upgraded RFX-mod: RFX-mod2 [52].

## 2. Materials and methods

2.1. Lithium wall conditioning

In RFX-mod, where particle control is particularly challenging [17], lithiumization was first

introduced with the LPI technique, where right-circular cylindrical (Ø = 1.5 mm, L = 5 mm)

lithium pellets were injected into He plasma discharges for ablation and distribution. Single

lithium pellet injection proved successful by improving density control and overall plasma

performance. The resulting Li coatings were uniform across the vessel. However, many time-

consuming He conditioning discharges were required in order to inject a sufficient amount of

Li [16].

Li evaporation was then tested via a CPS on loan from ENEA-Frascati laboratories, where it

was used in the FTU tokamak as a LLL. A full description of the LLL was given by Alfier et

al. [53]. While in past work the evaporator in RFX-mod was referred to as the LLL, we refer

to it herein as the CPS, since this more clearly reflects the function of the device in this work

as a Li evaporator. Briefly, the CPS is semi-cylindrical in shape with 120 cm2 of surface area.

Li is evaporated by heating the CPS to 450 C. In a given cycle, 1 g of Li can be evaporated in

90-120 mins. Prior to Li evaporation, the PFCs are exposed to extensive He GDC and He

plasma discharges [17]. While the CPS technique deposited orders of magnitude larger mass

of Li than the LPI technique, Li emission lines and initial SIMS measurements demonstrated

that the evaporated Li was highly non-uniform toroidally [17,18].

The latest Li conditioning technique tested, the MPI, sought to achieve the uniform Li coatings

achieved with the LPI technique but at a higher Li injection rate. The MPI was developed by

the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory and was described in detail by Mansfield et al. [54].

The MPI injects 1-mm Li spheres at a frequency of 250 Hz, which translates to 25

mg/discharge. This rate can be compared to the LPI Li injection rate of 4 mg/discharge. Li

emission lines and initial SIMS measurements demonstrated an improved spatial uniformity of

the MPI technique over the CPS technique [18].

2.2. Collector samples and dedicated manipulators

Three manipulators enable the exposure of samples to lithium deposition and are located at

three different toroidal positions. These toroidal manipulator positions are referred to as 9D,

11D, and 2D and are depicted in Figure 1. With respect to position 9D, positions 11D and 2D

2.3. Instrumental details

SIMS measurements and depth profiles of the species present were obtained by sputtering the

sample surface using a monoenergetic O2+ primary ion beam (6 keV, collimated to 50-µm dia.)

from a VG Fisons mass-filtered duoplasmatron ion gun (DP50B). The ion beam was rastered

over a 250 x 250-m area. A Hiden SIMS analyzer (EQS1000), using an electrostatic energy

analyzer and a quadrupole mass filter, was used in pulse counting mode for negative and

positive ion detection and collected ions from the central region (approx. 75%) of the rastered

area. At least five depth profiles were conducted on each sample from different locations to

confirm spatial uniformity, and only one of those depth profiles was then reported. The erosion

6

rate, measured by a KLA-Tencor mechanical surface profiler (P-10) with a 2-nm vertical

resolution, was 7 nm/min for the LPI and MPI samples and 27 nm/min for the CPS samples.

HR-XPS measurements, conducted in the Laboratory for Surface Chemistry (LSC) at Princeton

University, were performed in an ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) instrument equipped with a VG

Scienta XPS/UPS/ARPES/ISS hemispherical analyzer (R3000) with a 300-mm radius and a

position-sensitive detector based on a resistive anode channel plate system. A Scienta X-ray

source (MX 650) operated at 450 W and 15 kV and a 7-crystal monochromator provided Al K-

α X-rays (1486.7 eV). Ultimate performance of this instrument gave a Ag 3d5/2 peak with a

full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) of 0.60 eV. Samples were mounted on a Mo flag and

transferred to the analysis chamber (2×10-10 Torr). Spectra were obtained using a takeoff angle

of 90° for photoelectrons with respect to the surface plane of the sample. Survey scans of the

samples were obtained at a pass energy, Epass, of 200 eV (300 meV analyzer resolution), while

scans of smaller energy regions were obtained at Epass = 100 eV (150 meV analyzer resolution)

unless otherwise stated. For quantification, sensitivity factors of 0.025, 0.296, and 0.711 for Li

1s, C 1s, and O 1s, respectively, were used [56]. Reported binding energies (BEs) herein are

referenced to Au 4f7/2 at 84.0 eV BE. Sample charging was observed in the lithiated samples

and was corrected by shifting the raw data to align the Si 2p peak, which arises from the

overlapping 2p3/2 and 2p1/2 core lines, in the lithiated samples with the Si 2p peak (103.2 eV

BE) in a reference graphite sample that exhibited no charging. Sample charging in the lithiated

samples ranged from 0.3-0.9 eV. Si was an impurity found in all samples and is most likely

present as SiO2. Our Si 2p peak BE for SiO2 matches previously reported values [57]. Peak

fitting of HR-XPS spectra was performed in CasaXPS. The graphitic carbon C 1s peak was fit

using a Doniach-Šunjić function [58] with the FWHM allowed to vary as a fitting variable. All

other peaks were fit using mixed Gaussian-Lorentzian profiles with the FWHM of all peaks

within a given spectrum set to be equal. A Shirley background was used in all cases [59].

## 3. Results and discussion

3.1. SIMS measurements of lithium spatial and depth distributions

unused graphite sample (Figure 2a) and samples exposed to either the LPI, MPI, or CPS

lithiumization techniques at the 9D position (Figure 2b-d, respectively). Additional plots for

the 11D position can be found in the Supplementary Information. In the reference graphite

sample, the 7Li+ signal is at a background level (350 cps), while the 7Li+ signal is 104 times

larger in the samples exposed to Li conditioning. The 6Li+ signals were also recorded in the Li

conditioned samples to ensure that the Li isotope signals matched throughout the depth profile.

The 6Li+ and 7Li+ signals match in the LPI 9D sample in Figure 2b but cannot be compared for

the MPI 9D and CPS 9D samples in Figures 2c and 2d, respectively, since at the higher Li

levels in the MPI 9D and CPS 9D samples, the 7Li+ signal saturates the SIMS detector. Hence,

the 6Li+ signal is used to follow the Li depth profiles, as presented later in Figure 3.

The intensities of the 16O+ and 12C+ signals vary between samples and both show a trend of

MPI 9D > LPI 9D > reference graphite > CPS 9D, which matches that found in ref. [18]. The

12C+ intensity in the CPS 9D sample was 1-2 orders of magnitude lower than in the MPI 9D

and LPI 9D samples throughout the top 150 nm. The intensity of the 11B+ signal varied between

the samples with the following trend: MPI 9D > LPI 9D > CPS 9D ≈ reference graphite. The

11B+ signal increased significantly in the LPI and MPI samples as a result of contamination

from previous boron wall conditioning performed in RFX-mod. During the He discharge that

ablates and distributes the Li pellets, B in the graphite PFCs is sputtered and redeposited on the

LPI and MPI samples. The 11B+ signal in the CPS 9D sample remained at a background level

similar to the reference graphite sample since there was no plasma during Li evaporation.

Observation in Figure 2 of varying O, C, and B signals between the different Li conditioning

methods indicates that these samples probed by SIMS had significantly different chemical

environments, although we note that surface roughness and porosity could influence the

measured signals as well. Such different chemical environments, or matrix effects, are known

to cause changes in elemental ion yields, which makes quantifying SIMS data and comparing

elemental signals challenging between chemically different samples [60–62]. Oxygen, which

has a high electron affinity, introduces strong matrix effects in the surface that increase the ion

yield of positive ions. This known matrix effect of oxygen prompts us to evaluate the Li

concentration during the SIMS depth profiles by following the ratio of the 6Li+ signal to the

16O+ signal (6Li+/16O+). This approach has been used in past SIMS studies on RFX-mod samples

in efforts to limit the influence of oxygen matrix effects on depth profiles of Li, C, and B

[18,55]. Given that other unknown matrix effects influence the SIMS data as well, our

discussion of the SIMS results will be largely qualitative.

SIMS analysis of standards of known relevant mixtures of elemental concentrations and depth

profiles to provide calibrations, which was not possible for this report.

The poorer spatial uniformity of Li deposition observed for the MPI technique compared to the

LPI technique matches prior reports [18]. The decrease in spatial uniformity for the MPI

technique was attributed to the lower plasma penetration depth of the smaller Li pellets utilized

with the MPI technique (spherical; Ø = 1 mm) compared to the LPI technique (right-circular

cylindrical; Ø = 1.5 mm, L = 5 mm). High spatial nonuniformity between the CPS samples was

expected from past SIMS and Li influx studies in RFX-mod [17,18]. Innocente et al. reported

that proximity to the Li evaporator resulted in a thick Li film deposited on their 9D graphite

sample and a mixed Li/C film deposited on their 11D graphite sample [18].

By considering the plots shown in Figures 2 and 3, we can qualitatively describe how the

graphite samples were modified by the three Li conditioning techniques. With both the LPI and

MPI techniques, Li pellets are ablated during He discharges, and the resulting Li ions are

transported through the plasma and eventually implant in graphite. The Li concentration in the

graphite peaks within the top 60 nm, with Li intercalating more deeply into the bulk of the

graphite. With the CPS technique, graphite in close proximity to the evaporator (i.e. at position

9D) is coated by a thick layer of Li. Li intercalates into the graphite, but a significant Li film

remains at the graphite surface. In contrast, the CPS 11D sample, 60 away toroidally from the

evaporator, is coated with very little Li. The thin Li coating intercalates into the graphite bulk,

and no appreciable Li film is left at the graphite surface. This conclusion is supported by the

lack of a peak in the CPS 6Li+/16O+ ratio depth profiles and the low 6Li+/16O+ ratio for the CPS

11D sample.

Our assumption that there is a Li film on top of the graphite for the CPS 9D sample is supported

by the 6Li+/16O+ depth profiles in Figure 3a, the lower 12C+ signal for the CPS 9D sample

compared to the LPI 9D and MPI 9D samples in Figure 2, and the lack of a significant 11B+

signal in the CPS 9D sample compared to the LPI 9D and MPI 9D samples in Figure 2. This

proposal also explains several aspects of the B signal in the CPS 9D sample. Since the CPS 9D

sample was exposed to He GDC and He plasmas prior to Li evaporation, B from erosion and

redeposition is likely to be present in the graphite similar to what was seen for the LPI 9D and

MPI 9D samples in Figure 2b and 2c. However, no B signal was observed from the CPS 9D

sample substrate because of attenuation by the Li coating. In contrast, the CPS 11D sample full

3.2. HR-XPS measurements of surface elemental and chemical compositions

HR-XPS (hereafter indicated as XPS for brevity) survey spectra of unexposed graphite from

RFX-mod (used as a reference) and as-received post-exposure lithiated graphite samples are

shown in Figure 4. Each lithiated graphite sample was exposed to Li conditioning at the 9D

sample insertion position that is in the same toroidal section as the LPI and CPS and 30° away

toroidally from the MPI. The XPS survey scans are plotted on an absolute scale and have two

prominent peaks near 532 and 285 eV BE, corresponding to photoelectron emission from the

O 1s and C 1s core levels, respectively. In the lithiated graphite samples, Li (Li 1s, 56 eV BE)

was detected only for the CPS and MPI samples. The Li 1s peak for the MPI sample is difficult

to see at the scale used in Figure 4 but is readily observed in a regional scan in Figure 5. Si (Si

2s, 154 eV BE; Si 2p, 103 eV BE) and Na (Na KLL Auger, 498 eV BE) impurities were

detected for all samples. Na is a known impurity in RFX-mod graphite [44]. The XPS spectrum

from the unused graphite sample was dominated by a single, narrow graphitic C 1s peak at

284.65 eV BE (FWHM 0.7 eV), as shown in a regional XPS scan in Figure 5. XPS spectra

from the lithiated samples have a wider graphitic C peak and additional C peaks indicating

other chemical environments due to oxidized carbon species, which will be discussed further

below. Impurity oxygen in the unused graphite reference sample gave rise to an O 1s peak

centered at 532.9 eV BE. The lithiated samples showed a larger oxygen peak than the graphite

reference, which indicates an increased oxygen concentration at or near the surface due to

oxidation, as described quantitatively below in Table 2.

The surface elemental composition of the unexposed graphite and lithiated graphite samples

was obtained by quantitative XPS analysis and is shown in Table 2. This analysis determined

the average composition of the top several nm of the surface of the analyzed samples assuming

a homogeneous depth distribution of the detected elements. Calculations were carried out using

the expression Ci = (Ii/Si) / i(Ii/Si), where Ci is the concentration (atomic fraction), Ii is the

XPS signal intensity for each element, and Si is the atomic sensitivity factor for the measured

elemental core level [56]. The values for Ii were determined by integration of the individual

peak areas after appropriate background subtraction.

Lithium surface abundance was greatest for the CPS sample at 15 at.% Li, while only 3 at.%

Li was measured for the MPI sample. The difference in the amount of surface lithium between

the CPS and MPI samples is consistent with the difference in total injected Li for the two

samples. Li was not detected in the LPI sample by XPS, which was unexpected due to the

larger amount of Li injected with the LPI technique compared to the MPI technique for the

XPS samples (see Table 1). This disparity could again be a result of differences in the ablation,

plasma penetration, and transport of Li pellets in RFX-mod due to differences between the two

Li injection techniques in Li pellet size and the frequency of pellet injection. We note that

SIMS, contrary to XPS, did detect Li in the LPI 9D sample, and B in all of the 9D samples, but

that is not unexpected due to the differences in detection limits for XPS (0.1-1 at.%) and SIMS

(ppm-ppb) and sampling depths for the two techniques.

Oxygen levels in the lithiated graphite samples were notably higher than for the reference

graphite sample. We interpret the higher oxygen concentration in the lithiated samples as the

result of two effects. First, Li acted as a getter for oxygen-containing gases within the RFX-

mod vessel (i.e. H2O) and during sample exposure to ambient air. Second, background oxygen-

containing gases during the He GDC and He plasma discharges oxidized the graphite surface.

As stated above, He GDC and He plasma discharges were performed prior to Li evaporation

with the CPS, and He discharges were the method by which Li pellets were ablated and

transported for the LPI and MPI. While He is inert and thus does not oxidize the surface

directly, oxygen-containing gases increase in the background and are excited and ionized in

the He GDC and He plasma discharges, and so increased interaction and reaction of oxygen

with the initial graphite wall material results in increased oxygen levels in the lithiated graphite

samples.

In order to obtain further information on the chemical nature of the lithiated graphite sample

surfaces, we obtained narrow, regional scans of the XPS O 1s, C 1s, and Li 1s photoelectron

peaks from the lithiated graphite samples. These XPS regional scans for the LPI, MPI, and CPS

samples and the unexposed graphite reference are all presented in Figure 5, along with a

determination of the constituent peaks from decomposition of the overall intensity and

lineshape for each core level spectrum. Table 3 provides the BEs, FWHMs, and assignments

for these constituent peaks. The spectra in Figure 5 are displayed after being normalized to

have the same min to max intensities. All of the spectra were taken at Epass = 100 eV, except

for the LPI Li 1s spectrum, which was taken at Epass = 200 eV. To correct for the increased

intensity due to the two-fold higher pass energy, the intensity of the LPI Li 1s spectrum was

divided by a factor of ten, as intensity is proportional to Epass3.3 in our spectrometer.

In assigning the Li compounds that comprise the deposited Li film surfaces, we consider the

Li 1s spectra together with the C 1s and O1s spectra. A Li 1s peak was detected only for the

CPS and MPI samples. The CPS sample Li 1s peak is asymmetric and was best fit with two

peaks at 55.6 and 56.5 eV BE. Given that all the samples were exposed to ambient air between

Li injection and XPS analysis, surface Li is likely present as Li2CO3 [49,50,63–65]. Thus, for

the CPS sample, we assign the larger Li peak at 55.6 eV BE as due to Li2CO3, which is in close

agreement with reported Li binding energies for Li2CO3 of 55.4-55.5 eV  [64,66]. When

considering the BE separation of the accompanying C 1s and O 1s peaks from the Li 1s peak

for Li2CO3, as described by Wood and Teeter [65], our assignment of Li2CO3 is supported by

C 1s and O 1s peaks at 290.3 and 532.2 eV BE, respectively. Also, the Li 1s, C 1s, and O 1s

peak areas have the proper stoichiometric ratio for Li2CO3 after correction for the sensitivity

factors. We assign the second Li 1s peak in the CPS sample at 56.5 eV to lithium-intercalated

graphite, commonly denoted as LiC6. Assignment of this peak to metallic Li or other oxidized

Li compounds such as Li2O, LiOH, and Li2O2 was not preferred because the Li 1s BEs reported

for these compounds are lower than that of Li2CO3, not higher [40,63–66]. O 1s peaks for Li2O,

LiOH, and Li2O2 that have been reported to be 528.5-531.5 eV BE [42,49,50,64–66], were also

An unforeseen outcome of our HR-XPS regional scans of the lithiated samples was the clear

identification of the hydrogenated carbon peak at 285.1-285.2 eV BE from the graphitic carbon

peak at 284.3-284.4 eV BE in the C 1s spectra. While there are likely other contributions to the

intensity at or near the hydrogenated carbon peak (i.e. LiC6 in the CPS sample), our data

suggests a significant amount of the graphite in the top several nm is hydrogenated by the He

GDC and He discharges before any exposure to H-fueled discharges. The source of H could be

either H-containing residual vacuum gasses, i.e. H2 or H2O, or H that is sputtered and

redeposited from the surrounding H-containing, graphite PFCs of RFX-mod [77,78].

This observation of hydrogenation may seem counterintuitive as He GDC and He discharges

are known to reduce the net H content of graphite PFCs in RFX-mod and other fusion devices.

However, we again make the important distinction that our samples, contrary to fusion device

PFCs, had not yet been exposed to any H plasmas prior to He plasma exposure. Therefore, in

RFX-mod, He GDC/He discharges have the net effect of hydrogenating fresh graphite while

reducing, but not eliminating, H levels in H plasma-exposed graphite PFCs. Prior investigations

reported that increasing intensities of He ion bombardment [79] or baking [80] were required

to remove increasing amounts of H in graphite. Our XPS results suggest that He GDC/He

discharges in RFX-mod do not efficiently remove all of the tightly bound H in the graphite

Separately, the coexistence of Li2CO3 and LiC6 in the CPS XPS sample has important

implications. We know already from previous reports that Li2CO3 readily forms on the surface

of Li and Li compounds (i.e. Li2O, LiOH) when exposed to air. Our samples were exposed to

transfer from the vacuum transfer module to our HR-XPS chamber. The continued presence of

LiC6 in the sampling depth of our XPS measurements suggests that either (1) the Li2CO3 forms

an outer surface layer that grows to a finite depth and eventually acts as a diffusion barrier to

the reactant species H2O, CO2, and Li or (2) LiC6 is exposed through cracks in the Li2CO3 film

or cluster formation of Li2CO3. The coexistence of Li2CO3 and LiC6 XPS peaks after LiC6 was

detailed analysis of surface structure or morphology was not performed, but Ar+ ion sputtering

in our study shows that LiC6 remains in the top several nm of Li-exposed graphite even after

approximately one hour of air exposure.

## 4. Conclusions

This study used ex situ SIMS and XPS analysis to characterize and compare three

lithiumization techniques in RFX-mod by investigating the final elemental and chemical

compositions, depth profiles, and spatial uniformity of the surfaces resulting from Li

depositions on graphite samples. SIMS analysis determined that Li depositions were the most

uniform from the LPI technique, slightly less uniform from the MPI technique, and highly non-

uniform from the CPS technique. The LPI and MPI techniques appeared to implant Li into

graphite, while the CPS technique evaporated a Li film on top of the graphite with the thickness

highly dependent on proximity to the evaporator. With all of the techniques, Li intercalated

deep into the bulk of the graphite samples. Both SIMS and XPS analyses demonstrated that the

highest Li quantities were found in samples exposed to the CPS technique in the region closest

to the evaporator, followed by samples exposed to the MPI technique, and then the LPI

technique. Our SIMS results for the LPI and MPI techniques suggest that the spatial uniformity

of Li deposition in the torus improves with increasing Li pellet size, agreeing with prior reports.


<!-- Page 17 -->


17

We detected Li with XPS only in samples exposed to the MPI and CPS techniques. The XPS

spectra for the MPI and CPS samples exhibited peaks characteristic of Li2CO3, which formed

at the surface after sample exposure to atmospheric air. Our understanding of the chemical state

of surface Li in the RFX-mod vessel is convoluted by the observed formation of Li2CO3 in

atmospheric air, which supports the utilization of in vacuo surface analysis for Li plasma

material interactions studies. Peaks assigned to LiC6 in the Li 1s and C 1s XPS spectra were

only evident in the CPS sample. All of the lithiated samples showed evidence of hydrogenated

graphite, yet none of these samples were exposed to H-fueled plasma discharges. However,

each sample was exposed to He-fueled GDC or plasma discharges either during Li injection

(LPI and MPI techniques) or before Li evaporation (CPS technique). Given this sample history,

our results suggest that He GDC/He plasma discharges can hydrogenate fresh graphite samples,

which were previously unexposed to any plasma or Li conditioning. We propose that this

hydrogenation occurs via the bombardment of the fresh graphite sample surface with excited,

ionized, and/or dissociated H-containing gases (i.e. H2, H2O) from the residual vacuum or that

are evolved from the graphite tiles during He+ ion bombardment. The observed hydrogenation

in all of the XPS samples indicates that there are high levels of H in the RFX-mod vessel prior

to Li conditioning. In order to improve density control and the cleanliness of the injected or

evaporated Li, thereby improving plasma performance, we suggest more extensive He GDC or

He plasma discharge exposure before Li conditioning is performed.
